original_question: Which parasite, commonly associated with chorioretinitis in individuals with compromised immune systems, is also linked to hydrocephalus and cerebral calcifications when acquired congenitally?

final_qi.question: Which parasite, commonly associated with chorioretinitis in individuals with compromised immune systems, is also linked to hydrocephalus and cerebral calcifications when acquired congenitally?
final_qi.search_keyword: parasite chorioretinitis hydrocephalus cerebral calcifications congenital immune system
final_qi.long_answer: The parasite in question is Toxoplasma gondii. This parasite is commonly associated with chorioretinitis, especially in individuals with compromised immune systems. When acquired congenitally, Toxoplasma gondii infection can lead to the classic triad of symptoms in newborns, which includes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and cerebral calcifications. The congenital form of the disease, known as congenital toxoplasmosis, results from the transmission of the parasite from an infected mother to her fetus during pregnancy. In addition to these primary manifestations, congenital toxoplasmosis can also cause other complications such as seizures, developmental delays, and sensorineural hearing loss.

- Wikipedia: Information about: Toxoplasmosis
Section: Cause
Ingestion of raw or partly cooked meat, especially pork, lamb, or venison containing Toxoplasma cysts: Infection prevalence in countries where undercooked meat is traditionally eaten has been related to this transmission method. Tissue cysts may also be ingested during hand-to-mouth contact after handling undercooked meat, or from using knives, utensils, or cutting boards contaminated by raw meat.[47] Ingestion of unwashed fruit or vegetables that have been in contact with contaminated soil containing infected cat feces.[48] Ingestion of cat feces containing oocysts: This can occur through hand-to-mouth contact following gardening, cleaning a cat's litter box, contact with children's sandpits; the parasite can survive in the environment for months.[49] Ingestion of untreated, unfiltered water through direct consumption or utilization of water for food preparation.[50] Ingestion of unpasteurized milk and milk products, particularly goat's milk.[51] Ingestion of raw seafood.[52] Heart and lung transplants provide the highest risk for toxoplasmosis infection due to the striated muscle making up the heart,[45] which can contain cysts, and risks for other organs and tissues vary widely.[55] Risk of transmission can be reduced by screening donors and recipients prior to the transplant procedure and providing treatment.[55] Congenital toxoplasmosis is a specific form of toxoplasmosis in which an unborn fetus is infected via the placenta.[56] Congenital toxoplasmosis is associated with fetal death and miscarriage, and in infants, it is associated with hydrocephalus, cerebral calcifications and chorioretinitis, leading to encephalopathy and possibly blindness.[6] If a woman receives her first exposure to T. gondii while pregnant, the fetus is at particular risk.[6] A simple blood draw at the first prenatal doctor visit can determine whether or not a woman has had previous exposure and therefore whether or not she is at risk. A positive antibody titer indicates previous exposure and immunity, and largely ensures the unborn fetus' safety. Not much evidence exists around the effect of education before pregnancy to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis.[57] However educating parents before the baby is born has been suggested to be effective because it may improve food, personal and pet hygiene.[57] More research is needed to find whether antenatal education can reduce congenital toxoplasmosis.[57]
Section: Diagnosis
Lymph nodes affected by Toxoplasma have characteristic changes, including poorly demarcated reactive germinal centers, clusters of monocytoid B cells, and scattered epithelioid histiocytes.[citation needed] The classic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis includes: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial arteriosclerosis.[84] Other consequences include sensorineural deafness, seizures, and intellectual disability.[85] Congenital toxoplasmosis may also impact a child's hearing. Up to 30% of newborns have some degree of sensorineural hearing loss.[86] The child's communication skills may also be affected. A study published in 2010 looked at 106 patients, all of whom received toxoplasmosis treatment prior to 2.5 months. Of this group, 26.4% presented with language disorders.[87]
Section: Treatment
Pyrimethamine – an antimalarial medication. Sulfadoxine – an antibiotic used in combination (marketed as Fansidar) with pyrimethamine.
Combination therapy is usually given with folic acid supplements to reduce incidence of thrombocytopaenia.
Combination therapy is most useful in the setting of HIV. Spiramycin – an antibiotic used most often for pregnant women to prevent the infection of their children. Combination therapy is usually given with folic acid supplements to reduce incidence of thrombocytopaenia. Combination therapy is most useful in the setting of HIV. Atovaquone – an antibiotic that has been used to kill Toxoplasma cysts inside AIDS patients[91] Clindamycin – an antibiotic that, in combination with atovaquone, seemed to optimally kill cysts in mice[92]
Section: Epidemiology
Type I: virulent in mice and humans, seen in people with AIDS. Type II: non-virulent in mice, virulent in humans (mostly Europe and North America), seen in people with AIDS. Type III: non-virulent in mice, virulent mainly in animals but seen to a lesser degree in humans as well.
Section: Society and culture
Tennis player Arthur Ashe developed neurological problems from toxoplasmosis (and was later found to be HIV-positive).[114] Actor Merritt Butrick was HIV-positive and died from toxoplasmosis as a result of his already-weakened immune system.[115] Pedro Zamora, reality television personality and HIV/AIDS activist, was diagnosed with toxoplasmosis as a result of his immune system being weakened by HIV.[116] Prince François, Count of Clermont, pretender to the throne of France, had congenital toxoplasmosis; his disability caused him to be overlooked in the line of succession. Actress Leslie Ash contracted toxoplasmosis in the second month of pregnancy.[117] British middle-distance runner Sebastian Coe contracted toxoplasmosis in 1983, which was probably transmitted by a cat while he trained in Italy.[118][119] Tennis player Martina Navratilova experienced toxoplasmosis during the 1982 US Open.[120]

Section: Epidemiology
Type I: virulent in mice and humans, seen in people with AIDS. Type II: non-virulent in mice, virulent in humans (mostly Europe and North America), seen in people with AIDS. Type III: non-virulent in mice, virulent mainly in animals but seen to a lesser degree in humans as well.
Section: Society and culture
Tennis player Arthur Ashe developed neurological problems from toxoplasmosis (and was later found to be HIV-positive).[114] Actor Merritt Butrick was HIV-positive and died from toxoplasmosis as a result of his already-weakened immune system.[115] Pedro Zamora, reality television personality and HIV/AIDS activist, was diagnosed with toxoplasmosis as a result of his immune system being weakened by HIV.[116] Prince François, Count of Clermont, pretender to the throne of France, had congenital toxoplasmosis; his disability caused him to be overlooked in the line of succession. Actress Leslie Ash contracted toxoplasmosis in the second month of pregnancy.[117] British middle-distance runner Sebastian Coe contracted toxoplasmosis in 1983, which was probably transmitted by a cat while he trained in Italy.[118][119] Tennis player Martina Navratilova experienced toxoplasmosis during the 1982 US Open.[120]
